    Colour scaling, normalization and terrain shading¶

    Two fields with the same colormap can read completely differently depending on how values map to colours. cleopatra's ColorScaling group covers linear, power, symmetric-log, boundary and midpoint norms; Digital-Earth exposes them through the flat color_scale= keyword (plus gamma, bounds, midpoint). This notebook also shows hillshade for terrain relief.

    In [1]:
    Copied! 
    %matplotlib inline
from pathlib import Path
import numpy as np
from pyramids.dataset import Dataset, GeoReference
from digitalearth.scene import Map, grid

DATA = Path('../../../examples/data')   # notebook-relative path (docs/examples/presets -> repo root)
dem = Dataset.read_file(str(DATA / 'LisbonElevation.tif'))

# a strongly skewed positive field (a bright core over a faint background) where the scaling really matters
yy, xx = np.mgrid[0:120, 0:160]
blob = np.exp(-(((xx - 95)**2 + (yy - 45)**2) / (2 * 26**2)))
blob += 0.6 * np.exp(-(((xx - 55)**2 + (yy - 80)**2) / (2 * 18**2)))
skew = (blob * 5000 + 1).astype('float32')
GEO = (-180.0, 360 / 160, 0.0, 90.0, 0.0, -180 / 120)
skewed = Dataset.from_array(arr=skew, geo_ref=GeoReference(geo=GEO, epsg=4326))
    %matplotlib inline from pathlib import Path import numpy as np from pyramids.dataset import Dataset, GeoReference from digitalearth.scene import Map, grid DATA = Path('../../../examples/data') # notebook-relative path (docs/examples/presets -> repo root) dem = Dataset.read_file(str(DATA / 'LisbonElevation.tif')) # a strongly skewed positive field (a bright core over a faint background) where the scaling really matters yy, xx = np.mgrid[0:120, 0:160] blob = np.exp(-(((xx - 95)**2 + (yy - 45)**2) / (2 * 26**2))) blob += 0.6 * np.exp(-(((xx - 55)**2 + (yy - 80)**2) / (2 * 18**2))) skew = (blob * 5000 + 1).astype('float32') GEO = (-180.0, 360 / 160, 0.0, 90.0, 0.0, -180 / 120) skewed = Dataset.from_array(arr=skew, geo_ref=GeoReference(geo=GEO, epsg=4326))

    Linear vs power vs symmetric-log¶

    On a skewed field a linear scale spends almost all its colour on the few large values and washes the rest out. Power (gamma) and symmetric-log scales redistribute the colour so the low-value structure reappears.

    In [2]:
    Copied! 
    fig, maps = grid(1, 3, crs=4326, figsize=(15, 4))
for m, cs in zip(maps, ['linear', 'power', 'sym_log']):
    m.imshow(skewed, color_scale=cs, cmap='viridis'); m.set_title('color_scale=' + repr(cs))
fig;
    fig, maps = grid(1, 3, crs=4326, figsize=(15, 4)) for m, cs in zip(maps, ['linear', 'power', 'sym_log']): m.imshow(skewed, color_scale=cs, cmap='viridis'); m.set_title('color_scale=' + repr(cs)) fig;

    power takes a gamma (below 1 lifts the low end); tune it directly.

    In [3]:
    Copied! 
    fig, maps = grid(1, 2, crs=4326, figsize=(13, 4))
maps[0].imshow(skewed, color_scale='power', gamma=0.3, cmap='magma'); maps[0].set_title('power, gamma=0.3')
maps[1].imshow(skewed, color_scale='power', gamma=0.7, cmap='magma'); maps[1].set_title('power, gamma=0.7')
fig;
    fig, maps = grid(1, 2, crs=4326, figsize=(13, 4)) maps[0].imshow(skewed, color_scale='power', gamma=0.3, cmap='magma'); maps[0].set_title('power, gamma=0.3') maps[1].imshow(skewed, color_scale='power', gamma=0.7, cmap='magma'); maps[1].set_title('power, gamma=0.7') fig;

    Midpoint normalization for diverging data¶

    A diverging field should pin its neutral colour to a meaningful centre (usually zero). color_scale='midpoint' with midpoint= anchors the colormap there so positives and negatives stay balanced.

    In [4]:
    Copied! 
    lat = np.linspace(60, -60, 120)[:, None]; lon = np.linspace(-180, 180, 160)[None, :]
anom = (7 * np.sin(np.deg2rad(3 * lon)) * np.cos(np.deg2rad(2 * lat))).astype('float32')
anomaly = Dataset.from_array(arr=anom, geo_ref=GeoReference(geo=GEO, epsg=4326))
m = Map(crs=4326, figsize=(10, 5))
m.imshow(anomaly, color_scale='midpoint', midpoint=0, cmap='RdBu_r')
m.colorbar(label='anomaly'); m.set_title("color_scale='midpoint', midpoint=0"); m.fig;
    lat = np.linspace(60, -60, 120)[:, None]; lon = np.linspace(-180, 180, 160)[None, :] anom = (7 * np.sin(np.deg2rad(3 * lon)) * np.cos(np.deg2rad(2 * lat))).astype('float32') anomaly = Dataset.from_array(arr=anom, geo_ref=GeoReference(geo=GEO, epsg=4326)) m = Map(crs=4326, figsize=(10, 5)) m.imshow(anomaly, color_scale='midpoint', midpoint=0, cmap='RdBu_r') m.colorbar(label='anomaly'); m.set_title("color_scale='midpoint', midpoint=0"); m.fig;

    Boundary norm - explicit class breaks¶

    color_scale='boundary' with bounds=[...] maps values into discrete colour bands at breaks you choose - useful for legends with named classes.

    In [5]:
    Copied! 
    m = Map(crs=4326, figsize=(10, 5))
m.imshow(skewed, color_scale='boundary', bounds=[0, 50, 200, 1000, 3000, 5001], cmap='YlOrRd')
m.colorbar(label='value'); m.set_title("color_scale='boundary'"); m.fig;
    m = Map(crs=4326, figsize=(10, 5)) m.imshow(skewed, color_scale='boundary', bounds=[0, 50, 200, 1000, 3000, 5001], cmap='YlOrRd') m.colorbar(label='value'); m.set_title("color_scale='boundary'"); m.fig;

    Terrain relief with hillshade¶

    hillshade=True shades a raster by its slope and aspect. On its own it gives a grey relief; combined with an elevation preset it produces a shaded-relief elevation map.

    In [6]:
    Copied! 
    fig, maps = grid(1, 2, crs=dem.epsg, figsize=(13, 5))
maps[0].imshow(dem, hillshade=True, cmap='gray'); maps[0].set_title('hillshade')
maps[1].imshow(dem, style='elevation', hillshade=True); maps[1].set_title("style='elevation' + hillshade")
fig;
    fig, maps = grid(1, 2, crs=dem.epsg, figsize=(13, 5)) maps[0].imshow(dem, hillshade=True, cmap='gray'); maps[0].set_title('hillshade') maps[1].imshow(dem, style='elevation', hillshade=True); maps[1].set_title("style='elevation' + hillshade") fig;
